vulnerabilities.explanation: isGranted computes _currentBalance = token.balanceOf(_who) + lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who) and compares against plugin.minProposerVotingPower(). ground_truth.description: The MinVotingPowerCondition contract allows any users who hold at least plugin.minProposerVotingPower() amount of tokens (locked in the LockManager or in their token balance) to create a proposal and execute LockToVote.createProposal. This logic can be easily bypassed if the token allows flashloan or flashmint. Given that isGranted checks the user's token balance (line 45: token.balanceOf(_who) + lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who)), the user does not even need to lock the flashloaned amount into the LockManager to be able to create and spam proposals.

1. Flashloan the token.
2. Create the proposal (isGranted passes because token.balanceOf includes flashloaned amount).
3. Lock + vote the proposal and auto-execute it (EarlyExecution).
4. Unlock the tokens.
5. Repay the flashloan.

ground_truth.fix_description: Avoid using the token's balance and require the user to only use the locked amount. Change line 45 from 'token.balanceOf(_who) + lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who)' to just 'lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who)'. Store the proposal's creator in the proposal struct and require that the locked amount required to create the proposal won't be unlockable until the proposal ends.

vulnerabilities.explanation: totalControlled() calls oracle.latestRecord() and directly uses record.currentTotalValidatorBalance and record.cumulativeProcessedDepositAmount without any timestamp freshness check. ethToMETH() and mETHToETH() rely on this value for all mint/burn rate calculations.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Oracle record becomes stale after slashing (overstates totalControlled) or rewards (understates it). 2. Attacker calls stake() when totalControlled is understated to receive excess mETH. 3. Or calls unstakeRequest() when overstated to receive excess ETH. 4. Profit extracted from the mETH pool before oracle update.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: In totalControlled(), after fetching the record, require(block.timestamp - record.timestamp <= MAX_ORACLE_DELAY) and revert on stale data. Apply the same check in stake() and _unstakeRequest() before rate conversion.

ground_truth.description: Staking.totalControlled() derives the mETH/ETH exchange rate inputs from oracle.latestRecord() without validating the record timestamp. If the oracle lags significant state changes (e.g., validator rewards or slashing), the resulting rate becomes stale. An attacker can exploit this by timing mint/burn operations against outdated totals: redeeming mETH for excess ETH when a slashing is not yet reflected (overstated totalControlled()), or depositing ETH to mint excess mETH when recent rewards are not yet reflected (understated totalControlled()), extracting value from other users.

An attacker can exploit this by timing mint/burn operations against outdated totals: redeeming mETH for excess ETH when a slashing is not yet reflected (overstated totalControlled()), or depositing ETH to mint excess mETH when recent rewards are not yet reflected (understated totalControlled()), extracting value from other users.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
Slashing scenario:
1. Validators are slashed, reducing the actual ETH controlled by the protocol
2. Oracle has not yet updated to reflect the slashing
3. totalControlled() returns the old (higher) value
4. Attacker calls unstakeRequest() and receives more ETH per mETH than they should
5. Other users bear the loss when the oracle updates

Reward scenario:
1. Validators earn significant rewards
2. Oracle has not yet updated to reflect the new rewards
3. totalControlled() returns the old (lower) value
4. Attacker calls stake() and receives more mETH per ETH than they should
5. The mETH is worth more once the oracle updates
ground_truth.fix_description: Enforce freshness validation for oracle records when minting or burning mETH. The Oracle.latestRecord() function has no sanity checks - it simply returns _records[_records.length - 1]. The validations should be implemented on the caller side, specifically in the Staking.totalControlled() function.

vulnerabilities.explanation: In _unstakeRequest, mETHToETH(methAmount) is called at request time to fix ethRequested. This rate uses totalControlled() which includes liquidityBuffer.cumulativeDrawdown() and oracle data at that moment. The locked mETH is transferred to UnstakeRequestsManager but not burned, so it continues to participate in reward distribution via totalSupply() in mETHToETH. Subsequent slashing or returns are not applied to already-created requests.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. User A and User B both call unstakeRequest concurrently when rate is 1:1. 2. Oracle reports slashing, increasing cumulativeDrawdown. 3. User A (or MEV actor) front-runs claimUnstakeRequest to withdraw full ETH. 4. User B's claim reverts due to insufficient allocated ETH in UnstakeRequestsManager. Alternatively, pending requests dilute rewards for active stakers until claim burns the mETH.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Do not fix ethAmount at request time. Store only mETHLocked and compute ETH payout at claim time using current mETHToETH, ensuring slashing is socialized. Burn mETH at request time or exclude pending unstake shares from reward calculations.

ground_truth.description: When Staking.unstakeRequest() is called, the mETH/ETH rate is fixed and does not reflect slashing or rewards that may occur by the time Staking.claimUnstakeRequest() is executed. If two users create requests concurrently and losses arrive afterward, those losses are not socialized across them. One request may be fully paid while the other may revert on claim due to insufficient allocated funds. This can be exacerbated by frontrunning updates to LiquidityBuffer.cumulativeDrawdown(), enabling informed actors to anticipate loss application. Rewards are also misallocated: requests lock mETH but do not burn it until UnstakeRequestsManager.claim(), so these shares continue participating in reward distribution, diluting rewards for users who have not requested to unstake.

One request may be fully paid while the other may revert on claim due to insufficient allocated funds. ground_truth.attack_scenario:
Loss scenario:
1. Alice and Bob each hold 100 mETH, pool controls 200 ETH
2. Alice calls unstakeRequest(100 mETH), rate fixed at 1:1, expects 100 ETH
3. Bob calls unstakeRequest(100 mETH), rate fixed at 1:1, expects 100 ETH
4. Slashing event occurs, pool now only has 150 ETH
5. Protocol allocates 100 ETH to Alice's claim (succeeds)
6. Bob's claim reverts due to insufficient funds (only 50 ETH left)
7. The slashing loss was not socialized - Alice escaped, Bob bears full loss

Reward dilution scenario:
1. Alice and Bob each hold 100 mETH, pool controls 200 ETH
2. Alice calls unstakeRequest(100 mETH) - shares locked but not burned
3. 100 ETH reward is distributed across 200 mETH (all shares still exist)
4. Only ~50 ETH is attributed to Bob instead of ~100 ETH
5. Alice's locked shares continue to earn rewards until she claims
ground_truth.fix_description: Align withdrawal settlement with the latest protocol state to socialize slashing and adjust reward accounting so pending unstakes do not accrue or dilute rewards. The client acknowledged this as a protocol design trade-off.

vulnerabilities.explanation: validateUserOp performs an external self-call `this.isValidSignature(...)` (line 36). This changes msg.sender from entrypoint to the wallet contract itself. BaseAuth.signatureValidation (called via isValidSignature) enforces static signature caller binding with `if (addr != address(0) && addr != msg.sender) revert InvalidStaticSignatureWrongCaller`. Static signatures explicitly bound to the entrypoint therefore always revert.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario:
1. User creates static signature bound to entrypoint address via setStaticSignature.
2. User submits UserOperation through ERC-4337 entrypoint.
3. validateUserOp executes the external isValidSignature call.
4. signatureValidation sees msg.sender == wallet (not entrypoint) and reverts with InvalidStaticSignatureWrongCaller.
5. UserOperation validation fails permanently for any static-signature user.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Replace the external self-call with an internal call: `if (!isValidSignature(userOpHash, userOp.signature)) return SIG_VALIDATION_FAILED;` or propagate the intended caller (entrypoint) into signatureValidation so static-signature checks use the original caller.

vulnerabilities.explanation: beforeSwap computes the quote digest via keccak256(abi.encode(sender, key, params.zeroForOne, maxAmountIn, maxExchangeRate, exchangeRateDenom, nonce, expiryTime)) with no chainid, contract address, or EIP-712 domain separator. The same PoolKey can exist on multiple chains via CREATE3 deployment, so any valid signature+nonce from chain A is accepted on chain B.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario:
1. Attacker obtains a valid signed quote (signature, nonce, expiry) for a swap on chain A.
2. Deploys identical hook contract on chain B using same CREATE3 salt so PoolKey matches.
3. Submits identical hookData containing the signature to beforeSwap on chain B.
4. SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow succeeds because digest matches, nonce is unused on B, and swap executes without signer's authorization on chain B.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Wrap the digest in EIP-712 typed data using an EIP712Domain struct that includes chainId, verifyingContract address, and name/version. Compute digest with _hashTypedDataV4 and require signatures only on the intended chain.

ground_truth.description: Both UniswapV4KEMHook and PancakeSwapInfinityKEMHook rebuild a quote digest by hashing sender, key, params.zeroForOne, maxAmountIn, maxExchangeRate, exchangeRateDenom, nonce, and expiryTime. The tuple ties the authorization to the router (sender), the full PoolKey (which includes the hook address), trade direction, price and input caps, nonce and expiry. Crucially, no domain separator is folded in: chain ID, deployment salt, and contract identity outside key are absent. If the same hook instance (or the same PoolKey) is deployed on multiple networks, as CREATE3-based salt mining allows, an attacker can lift any valid signature+nonce from chain A and replay it on chain B. Because the digest matches, SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow succeeds and the swap executes without the signer's intention. That breaks the core guarantee that signed quotes are single-instance authorizations, allowing cross-chain replay swaps.

ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. Kyber deploys UniswapV4KEMHook on Ethereum mainnet with a specific PoolKey
2. Same hook (or same PoolKey configuration) is deployed on Arbitrum using CREATE3 salt mining to get matching address
3. User requests a quote on Ethereum, quoteSigner signs: keccak256(abi.encode(sender, key, zeroForOne, maxAmountIn, maxExchangeRate, exchangeRateDenom, nonce, expiryTime))
4. User broadcasts swap transaction on Ethereum mainnet
5. Attacker observes the transaction in Ethereum mempool, extracts signature and hookData
6. Attacker submits identical calldata on Arbitrum before expiryTime
7. On Arbitrum: sender (router) matches, key matches (same pool configuration), all other parameters match
8. SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow(quoteSigner, digest, signature) returns true
9. Swap executes on Arbitrum without signer's intention
10. If nonce != 0, Ethereum swap may still succeed (different nonce storage per chain), causing double execution
ground_truth.fix_description: Introduce domain separation for the signed payload in both hooks. Adopt an EIP712 domain that at minimum commits to chainid. This ensures signatures are only valid on the intended chain.

vulnerabilities.explanation: isGranted computes voting power as token.balanceOf(_who) + lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who). balanceOf returns the raw ERC20 balance without verifying transferability. Tokens that are frozen or blacklisted (USDC/USDT) remain countable even though _lock() and _doLockTransfer() will revert on transfer attempts.

3. Permission check invokes isGranted, which reads balanceOf returning the full amount.
4. Check passes and proposal is created despite attacker being unable to lock or transfer any tokens.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Remove token.balanceOf(_who) from the check. Only use lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who) (which reflects tokens actually transferred into the LockManager) as the source of voting power.

vulnerabilities.explanation: Signature validation in beforeSwap computes digest = keccak256(abi.encode(sender, key, ...)) where sender is the router address passed by PoolManager. SignatureChecker validates against quoteSigner using only this router-bound data plus nonce/expiry. No original user address is included or retrieved via router.msgSender().
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Alice obtains valid signed hookData for a swap and broadcasts tx through Kyber router. 2. MEV bot reads mempool calldata (hookData + signature). 3. Bot submits identical calldata first via same router; beforeSwap accepts it, _useUnorderedNonce consumes nonce. 4. Alice's tx reverts on nonce reuse. Bot executes dust swap to invalidate quote.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Modify signature to include original caller: retrieve via router.msgSender() (or equivalent) and encode it in the digest instead of (or in addition to) the router sender address.

ground_truth.description: Both hooks accept swaps when SignatureChecker validates keccak256(abi.encode(sender, key, ..., nonce, expiryTime)). The sender field is the router contract that called the pool manager. That restricts execution to Kyber's router, but not to any particular user. Because the router is public, anyone can forward the calldata and signature. If Alice broadcasts a signed swap, an MEV bot can copy the calldata, submit it first and the hook sees the same router address and quote terms: the attacker's swap succeeds, consuming the nonce. Alice's transaction then reverts at _useUnorderedNonce because the nonce is already marked as used. The attacker, this way, can invalidate the quote with a dust swap. Designers intended router-level exclusivity, yet end users receive no front-running protection, exposing every quote to mempool sniping.

ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. Alice requests a quote from Kyber backend for swapping 100 ETH -> USDC
2. Kyber quoteSigner signs the quote with parameters: sender=router, maxAmountIn=100e18, maxExchangeRate, nonce=12345, expiryTime=now+60s
3. Alice constructs swap transaction and broadcasts to mempool
4. MEV bot observes Alice's pending transaction, extracts hookData containing signature
5. Bot constructs identical swap call through same router with minimal amountSpecified (e.g., 0.001 ETH)
6. Bot submits with higher gas price, gets included first
7. Hook.beforeSwap() validates: sender=router (matches), signature valid, nonce 12345 unused -> swap succeeds
8. _useUnorderedNonce(12345) marks nonce as used
9. Alice's transaction executes next: same signature, same nonce
10. _useUnorderedNonce(12345) reverts with NonceAlreadyUsed(12345)
11. Alice's swap fails, bot successfully griefed the quote (or profited if quote was favorable)
ground_truth.fix_description: Include the router's original caller in the signature. The original caller can be retrieved by the hook by calling router.msgSender() function. This ensures the signature is bound to a specific end user, not just the router contract.

ground_truth.description: If the Midas vault admin calls rejectRequest() on a pending redemption request, the request status is set to Cancelled and the user's mTokens remain locked in the Midas vault. The Midas admin can transfer these mTokens back to any address, especially to the Gateway (which created the request). However, even if mTokens are transferred back to the Gateway, there's no mechanism to recover them from the Gateway to the user's credit account. Additionally, if mTokens are sent to the credit account or any address other than the Gateway, pendingTokenOutAmount() will continue to show a non-zero result despite the request being rejected, inflating the phantom token's balance and the credit account's collateral value.

The Midas admin can transfer these mTokens back to any address, especially to the Gateway (which created the request). However, even if mTokens are transferred back to the Gateway, there's no mechanism to recover them from the Gateway to the user's credit account. ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. User creates a credit account and deposits mTokens
2. User calls redeemRequest() through the adapter, which calls the Gateway's requestRedeem()
3. Gateway records the pending redemption in pendingRedemptions[creditAccount] with isActive=true
4. Midas vault admin (external trusted party) calls rejectRequest() on the pending request
5. Request status in Midas vault is set to Cancelled, but mTokens remain locked in Midas vault
6. Gateway's pendingRedemptions mapping still shows isActive=true
7. pendingTokenOutAmount() returns non-zero value based on stale mTokenRate calculation
8. Phantom token balanceOf() returns inflated value
9. Credit account's collateral appears higher than actual recoverable value
10. Consequences: (a) User funds permanently blocked with no recovery mechanism, (b) Inflated collateral can be exploited for additional borrowing, (c) If mTokens are sent back to Gateway, they're stuck with no transfer mechanism
ground_truth.fix_description: Implement functionality to handle rejected requests, allowing the system to clear rejected requests and transfer tokens out of the Gateway. The fix added manual processing capability for rejected requests to allow market curator collaboration with Midas to recover withdrawals.

If the current default manager is deactivated via LiquidityBuffer.updatePositionManager()/togglePositionManagerStatus() without first switching defaultManagerId or disabling auto-allocation, _allocateETHToManager(defaultManagerId, …) reverts with LiquidityBuffer__ManagerInactive(). ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. Admin sets defaultManagerId to manager 0 with shouldExecuteAllocation = true
2. Admin calls togglePositionManagerStatus(0) to deactivate the default manager

4. depositETH() calls _allocateETHToManager(defaultManagerId, msg.value)

vulnerabilities.explanation: unlock() executes 'delete lockedUntil' (setting it to 0) before transferring LP tokens. The transfer triggers fee crediting to the locker via the V2 pool. claimFees() is guarded by onlyLocked (requires lockedUntil != 0), so post-unlock the contract can never call claimFees() again, stranding all accumulated fees.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. User locks LP and earns fees over time. 2. User calls unlock(_recipient) without first calling claimFees(). 3. lockedUntil is deleted. 4. LP transfer credits new fees to locker. 5. Any subsequent claimFees() reverts with NotLocked. Fees remain permanently in the contract with no withdrawal path.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: In unlock(), call _claimFees({_recipient: _recipient}) (or equivalent) before deleting lockedUntil to distribute all pending fees to the recipient.

ground_truth.description: The Locker.claimFees() function is protected by the onlyLocked modifier, which requires lockedUntil != 0. Inside V2Locker.unlock(), the contract sets lockedUntil = 0 (via delete lockedUntil) before transferring the LP tokens to the recipient. During the LP token transfer, the underlying pool credits all accumulated fees to the locker contract. Once the LP tokens are transferred out, the locker can no longer call claimFees() because it is no longer locked (lockedUntil == 0), leaving those fees permanently stranded on the contract. A user who forgets to call claimFees() before unlocking will lose the entire fee balance earned up to that moment.

ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. User creates a V2Locker and deposits LP tokens into a Velodrome V2 pool
2. Over time, the pool accumulates trading fees for the locker
3. The lock period expires and the user calls unlock() to retrieve their LP tokens
4. Inside unlock(), lockedUntil is set to 0 on line 46
5. The LP tokens are transferred to the recipient on line 48
6. During this transfer, the V2Pool.claimFees() is implicitly called, crediting fees to the locker contract
7. User realizes they forgot to claim fees and tries to call claimFees()
8. claimFees() reverts with NotLocked() because lockedUntil == 0 (onlyLocked modifier check fails)
9. The accumulated fees (token0 and token1) are permanently stuck on the locker contract with no way to retrieve them
ground_truth.fix_description: Claim swap fees within the V2Locker.unlock() function before setting lockedUntil to 0. This ensures all accumulated fees are sent to the recipient before the lock state is cleared.

vulnerabilities.explanation: The function uses plugin.isProposalOpen(_proposalId) to decide whether to remove a proposal from knownProposalIds. isProposalOpen() returns false both when a proposal has ended and when it has not yet started. Future-start proposals are therefore removed during any unlock() call.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario:
1. Plugin creates a proposal with startDate in the future; proposalCreated adds it to knownProposalIds.
2. User with locked tokens calls unlock() before startDate.
3. _withdrawActiveVotingPower sees !isProposalOpen() and removes the ID.
4. After startDate, user votes on the proposal.
5. Later unlock() no longer iterates the proposal, skips clearVote, and succeeds while voting power remains recorded in the plugin, allowing token withdrawal without clearing the vote.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Replace the check with a new isProposalEnded() that returns true only after endDate has passed or the proposal is executed. Keep isProposalOpen() for voting eligibility checks.

ground_truth.description: The isProposalOpen() function returns true if a proposal is open for voting. It returns false if it's too late OR too early for voting. But in _withdrawActiveVotingPower() at line 225, it was being used as an 'isProposalStillOpen()' function, forgetting that it will also be false when the proposal hasn't started yet. This means proposals with future start dates get incorrectly removed from knownProposalIds tracking.

ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. A proposal is created with a future start date (e.g., starts in 1 week).
2. User calls unlock() before the proposal starts.
3. _withdrawActiveVotingPower() is called at line 135.
4. Line 225: plugin.isProposalOpen(_proposalId) returns false (proposal hasn't started).
5. Line 226: knownProposalIds.remove(_proposalId) - proposal removed from tracking.
6. Proposal starts a week later, user votes.
7. User calls unlock() again - vote isn't cleared because proposal isn't tracked.
8. User withdraws tokens while still having active votes.
ground_truth.fix_description: Create and use an isProposalEnded() function specifically for this use case. It should return true only if the proposal has actually ended (endDate passed or executed), not just because it hasn't started.

ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. A 'normal' proposal_1 is created ending in 1 year.
2. Alice locks 100 tokens, votes NO on proposal_1.
3. Attacker creates proposal_2 with action: LockManager.proposalEnded(proposal_1_id).
4. proposal_2 passes and executes.
5. proposalEnded(proposal_1) is called via delegatecall from the plugin.
6. proposal_1 is removed from knownProposalIds.

ground_truth.fix_description: Remove the realizedPremium != 0 guard. Derive commission directly from premium when shortAmount == 0 && longAmount == 0.

1. Configurator sets up phantom token A tracking output token USDC via setTokenAllowedStatusBatch()
2. phantomTokenToOutputToken[phantomA] = USDC
3. User makes a redemption request for output token USDT (different from USDC)
4. pendingRedemptions records the request with tokenOut = USDT
5. User calls withdrawPhantomToken(phantomA, amount)

7. Function calls _withdraw(amount) which executes Gateway.withdraw()

vulnerabilities.explanation: Raw IERC20.transferFrom() and transfer() calls ignore return values. 2. erc20Token.transferFrom returns false (no revert).
3. lockedBalances[msg.sender] += _amount still executes.
4. Attacker obtains arbitrary voting power in downstream plugins without depositing tokens.
5. Repeat to drain governance influence.

Some ERC20 tokens like BAT, HT, cUSDC, ZRX do not revert when a transfer fails but instead return false.

1. Attacker specifies an arbitrary _amount without having ever given any approval.
2. erc20Token.transferFrom() returns false but doesn't revert.

vulnerabilities.explanation: deposit() calls calculateShares(amount) which returns (amount * totalSupply) / totalAssets and can round down to 0 when totalAssets >> totalSupply. It then mints without checking shares > 0. receivePenaltyReward() is public and allows any caller to call deposit_for on the veNFT, inflating totalAssets without minting shares.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker deposits 1 wei HYBR, receives 1 gHYBR share (1:1). 2. Attacker calls receivePenaltyReward(1000e18) or uses deposit_for via votingEscrow to donate 1000e18 HYBR. 3. Victim calls deposit(100e18). 4. calculateShares returns (100e18 * 1) / 1000e18e18 = 0. 5. Victim receives 0 shares; attacker now owns 1 share worth 1100e18 HYBR.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: In deposit(), add `uint256 shares = calculateShares(amount); require(shares > 0, "Zero shares");` before _mint. Add `onlyOwner` or similar access control to receivePenaltyReward().

ground_truth.description: The gHYBR contract is just another veNFT position holder from the perspective of votingEscrow contract, while the gHYBR contract acts as a vault. And the deposit does not ensure that we mint at least one gHYBR share. This can lead to a condition where the first depositor attacks another user. Example: - Alice deposits dust shares, 1 share : 1 asset - Alice donates 1000e18 assets before Bob deposits, through deposit_for, and he increased the ratio by 1 shares : 1000e18 assets - Bob deposits 100e18 assets, the shares calculation goes 100e18 * 1 / 1000e18 and rounds down to 0 - Receives 0 shares - All bob’s deposit is captured by Alice’s shares - Bob deposits 100e18 assets and receives 0 shares - Alice has 1 share worth 1000e18 + 100e18(bob's) assets The entry points the attacker can use to perform this attack are: 1. The votingEscrow contract allows anyone to deposit assets for any position through its public deposit_for(uint _tokenId, uint _value) external nonreentrant function. 2. The receivePenaltyReward function in GovernanceHYBR contract lacks access control, which allows an attacker to donate to increase totalAssets. 3. Attacker can utilize multiSplit through withdraw, by first depositing 1000:1000 and withdrawing so that the leftover is 1:1 ratio dust. Impact: Alice captures all of Bob’s deposits.

ground_truth.attack_scenario: function test_submissionValidity() external { // first depositor attack address alice = makeAddr("alice"); address bob = makeAddr("bob"); vm.startPrank(address(minter)); hybr.mint(alice, 2000e18); hybr.mint(bob, 100e18); vm.stopPrank(); vm.startPrank(alice); hybr.approve(address(gHybr), type(uint).max); gHybr.deposit(2, alice); hybr.transfer(address(gHybr), 1000e18); // alice transfers 1000 HYBR to gHYBR gHybr.receivePenaltyReward(1000e18); // alice donates 1000 through the receivePenaltyReward function vm.stopPrank(); // bob deposits vm.startPrank(bob); hybr.approve(address(gHybr), 100e18); gHybr.deposit(100e18, bob); vm.stopPrank(); console.log("alice's shares: ", gHybr.balanceOf(alice)); console.log("bob's shares: ", gHybr.balanceOf(bob)); console.log("gHYBR total assets: ", gHybr.totalAssets()); } Run this test and see the result: - Alice’s shares: 2 - Bob’s shares: 0 - gHYBR total assets: 1100000000000000000002 Alice captures all of Bob’s deposits.

vulnerabilities.location: BaseSig library: recover() lines 88-106 and recoverChained()
vulnerabilities.explanation: When signatureFlag bit 6 (0x40) is unset in a chained signature (bit 0 set), recover() skips the entire checkpointer block, leaving _checkpointer=address(0) and snapshot.imageHash=bytes32(0). recoverChained() then calls recover() with _ignoreCheckpointer=true and never enforces the checkpointer, allowing validation to succeed with snapshot.imageHash==0.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker (evicted signer) crafts chained signature with bit 6=0. 2. Calls recover() on payload using stale config. 3. recoverChained processes segments without checkpointer validation. 4. Final imageHash check passes because _snapshot remains zero-valued. 5. Unauthorized operation executes.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: In recover(), before calling recoverChained when bit 0 is set, add: if (signatureFlag & 0x40 == 0) revert MissingCheckpointer(); Ensure checkpointer is always required for chained signatures.

ground_truth.description: When a wallet is behind a checkpointer and a chained signature is used with bit 6 (checkpointer usage flag) set to zero, BaseSig.recover skips the checkpointer validation block (BaseSig.sol:88-106). This leaves _checkpointer and snapshot unset (zero-valued). In recoverChained, the checkpointer is ignored, and the signature validation passes even if the checkpointer should be enforced. The final validation succeeds because snapshot.imageHash == bytes32(0) as the checkpointer is ignored.
ground_truth.root_cause: When a wallet is behind a checkpointer and a chained signature is used with bit 6 (checkpointer usage flag) set to zero, BaseSig.recover skips the checkpointer validation block (BaseSig.sol:88-106). This leaves _checkpointer and snapshot unset (zero-valued). In recoverChained, the checkpointer is ignored, and the signature validation passes even if the checkpointer should be enforced. The final validation succeeds because snapshot.imageHash == bytes32(0) as the checkpointer is ignored.
ground_truth.attack_scenario: An evicted signer can sign a payload valid under stale wallet configuration and bypass checkpointer validation. PoC: Add test case to BaseSigTest and run forge test --match-test test_PoC_checkpointer_bypass. The test constructs a chained signature with checkpointer disabled, mocks the checkpointer response, and asserts successful recovery with correct image hash.

vulnerabilities.explanation: claimRewards calls `IVoter(voter).poolVote(veTokenId)` to retrieve voted pools. In VoterV3.sol, `poolVote` is defined as `mapping(uint256 => address[]) public poolVote`. The public getter for this mapping accepts a uint256 key and returns a single address[] value, but the call pattern and interface usage in the provided code causes an invalid call that reverts at runtime (as documented in the benchmark). Subsequent bribe-claiming logic is unreachable.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario:
1. Operator calls claimRewards().
2. Execution reaches `address[] memory votedPools = IVoter(voter).poolVote(veTokenId)`.
3. Call reverts due to incorrect mapping access.
4. No rebase or bribe rewards can ever be claimed; rewards remain stuck in bribes/gauge contracts.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Add `function getPoolVote(uint256) external view returns (address[] memory);` (or equivalent) to the IVoter interface and VoterV3 implementation that explicitly returns `poolVote[tokenId]`. Update claimRewards to use the new getter.

ground_truth.description: `claimRewards()` uses `IVoter.poolVote(veTokenId)` incorrectly; `poolVote` is a mapping, not a function returning an array, causing a revert.
ground_truth.root_cause: `claimRewards()` uses `IVoter.poolVote(veTokenId)` incorrectly; `poolVote` is a mapping, not a function returning an array, causing a revert.
ground_truth.attack_scenario: A test votes on pools, warps time, and `claimRewards()` reverts due to invalid getter call.
ground_truth.fix_description: Add `getPoolVote(veTokenId)` in `VoterV3.sol` to return the array. Status: Mitigation confirmed.

vulnerabilities.explanation: The expression `uint256(_currentResiduals << 12)` places the 96-bit residuals at bits 12-107. This overlaps the referenceTick field (bits 96-117). The subsequent addition of `(referenceTick << 96)` causes bit corruption in both fields due to carry and overlap.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario:
1. Call insertObservation (or any path invoking storeOraclePack) with a valid newTick.
2. The corrupted OraclePack is written back.
3. Subsequent calls to lastTick, getMedianTick, residualTick, or getEMAs read garbage values.
4. Median/EMA prices become incorrect, enabling mispricing in any contract consuming the oracle.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Change to `uint256(_currentResiduals)` (shift 0) so residuals occupy bits 0-95, with latestResidual occupying bits 0-11 and the prior 7 residuals in bits 12-95. Verify all shifts against the documented layout.

vulnerabilities.explanation: unstakeRequestWithPermit unconditionally calls SafeERC20Upgradeable.safePermit(mETH, msg.sender, address(this), methAmount, deadline, v, r, s) before _unstakeRequest. The mETH permit uses a nonce that is consumed on first use. An attacker monitoring the mempool can extract v/r/s and call mETH.permit() first, incrementing the nonce and invalidating the signature.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario:
1. User broadcasts unstakeRequestWithPermit(tx) containing a valid permit signature.
2. Attacker reads mempool, extracts v/r/s/deadline.
3. Attacker calls mETH.permit(user, Staking, amount, deadline, v, r, s) in a higher-gas tx; permit succeeds and nonce advances.
4. User's tx executes, safePermit reverts with invalid signature/nonce.
5. User's unstake is blocked even though allowance may already exist.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Wrap the permit call in try/catch: try SafeERC20Upgradeable.safePermit(...) {} catch {} then proceed with _unstakeRequest only if allowance >= methAmount (or use a non-reverting permit check).

ground_truth.description: An attacker can read the v, r, s from the mempool and call mETH.permit() first, consuming the user's signature and updating the nonce. The subsequent user transaction Staking.unstakeRequestWithPermit() then reverts on the permit() call due to an invalidated signature/nonce, preventing the unstake flow from executing, even though allowance is already set.
ground_truth.root_cause: An attacker can read the v, r, s from the mempool and call mETH.permit() first, consuming the user's signature and updating the nonce. The subsequent user transaction Staking.unstakeRequestWithPermit() then reverts on the permit() call due to an invalidated signature/nonce, preventing the unstake flow from executing, even though allowance is already set.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. User submits unstakeRequestWithPermit() transaction with signature (v, r, s) to the mempool
2. Attacker monitors mempool and extracts the permit signature parameters
3. Attacker front-runs with a direct call to mETH.permit() using the extracted (v, r, s)
4. The permit succeeds, consuming the user's nonce and setting the allowance
5. User's original unstakeRequestWithPermit() transaction is mined
6. The SafeERC20Upgradeable.safePermit() call inside unstakeRequestWithPermit() reverts because the nonce is already used
7. User's unstake request fails even though the allowance was set
ground_truth.fix_description: Wrap the permit() invocation in a try-catch clause and proceed with the unstake if allowance is already sufficient, avoiding a hard revert when signatures are pre-consumed.

vulnerabilities.explanation: deploy() performs CREATE2 and unconditionally reverts with DeployFailed when the resulting address is zero (which occurs on CREATE2 collision). No check for pre-existing code at the predicted address is performed, violating the ERC-4337 expectation that deploy returns the existing address instead of reverting.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker observes a pending deploy(_mainModule, _salt) tx. 2. Attacker front-runs with identical parameters, causing the first deployment to succeed. 3. Victim's tx now hits the collision path and reverts. 4. Repeated front-running prevents any subsequent deploy calls for that salt, breaking wallet creation and bundler simulations.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Before CREATE2, compute the predicted address with keccak256(0xff || address(this) || _salt || keccak256(code)). If that address already has code (extcodesize > 0), return it directly; otherwise proceed with CREATE2.

ground_truth.description: Factory.deploy uses create2 but reverts with CreateCollision if address exists, violating ERC-4337 expectation to return address. Breaks simulations and bundler logic.
ground_truth.root_cause: Factory.deploy uses create2 but reverts with CreateCollision if address exists, violating ERC-4337 expectation to return address. Breaks simulations and bundler logic.
ground_truth.attack_scenario: Deploy wallet once, call deploy again → reverts. Attacker can front-run to cause DoS. PoC: test_factory_double_deploy_PoC in AuditPoC.sol. Shows first deploy succeeds, second reverts.
ground_truth.fix_description: Check if address exists via predicted.code.length, return it if so.

The emergencyTokenTransfer function allows unrestricted transfer of any ERC20 token, including aWETH which represents the protocol's position in Aave.
ground_truth.root_cause: EMERGENCY_ROLE in PositionManager can transfer aWETH from the contract to any address without restrictions, which may be unintended and creates additional risks in case this role is compromised. The emergencyTokenTransfer function allows unrestricted transfer of any ERC20 token, including aWETH which represents the protocol's position in Aave.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. Attacker compromises the account holding EMERGENCY_ROLE
2. Attacker calls emergencyTokenTransfer(aWETH, attackerAddress, aWETH.balanceOf(positionManager))
3. All aWETH tokens (representing ETH deposited in Aave) are transferred to the attacker
4. Protocol loses all funds deposited through this position manager
5. The attack bypasses the normal withdraw() flow which goes through LiquidityBuffer
ground_truth.fix_description: Disallow aWETH emergency transfers or approvals from the PositionManager contract, since withdrawals are already handled via the more transparent withdraw() flow. The team acknowledged this is intentional for rapid fund withdrawal in critical situations and noted EMERGENCY_ROLE will not be configured at launch.

vulnerabilities.explanation: When create_lock + increase_amount (or multiple deposits) occur in one tx, _checkpoint appends a new point_history entry with identical timestamp to the prior one instead of overwriting. balanceOfNFT uses the latest point by timestamp; duplicate ts causes it to read stale slope/bias, under-calculating voting power.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Alice calls create_lock(500e18, ...) then increase_amount(tokenId, 500e18) in same tx. 2. _deposit_for calls _checkpoint twice with same block.timestamp. 3. Second checkpoint writes point_history[epoch] at same ts. 4. balanceOfNFT reads the first (pre-increase) point, returning ~half expected votes. 5. Bribe/reward calculations using votes distribute less to Alice.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: In _checkpoint after computing last_point, if point_history[_epoch].ts == block.timestamp then overwrite it; else append and increment epoch.

ground_truth.description: `_checkpoint` creates a new epoch with the same timestamp for `increase_amount`, ignoring the new lock in `balanceOfNFT`, reducing voting power.

ground_truth.attack_scenario: A test locks 500e18, increases by 500e18 in one tx, and shows reduced bribe rewards compared to separate locks.
ground_truth.fix_description: In `_checkpoint`, overwrite the latest point if timestamps match, else append a new one. Status: Mitigation confirmed.

ground_truth.attack_scenario: Original payload: Calls [A, B, C] with signatures [SigA, SigB, SigC]. Execution: [A succeed, B succeed, C revert]. Result: Revert, nonce unused. vulnerabilities.explanation: In _vote(), after _reset(), the loop computes _poolWeight = _weights[i] * _weight / _totalVoteWeight then executes require(_poolWeight != 0, "ZV"). When a user has previously cast a 1-wei dust vote on a pool, any subsequent decay of veNFT balance causes the multiplication+division to underflow to 0 on poke(), making the require fail and reverting the entire poke().
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker calls vote() with weights [W-1, 1] on two live pools. 2. Time passes and veNFT balance decays. 3. Any party (including via ve.deposit_for) calls poke(_tokenId). 4. _vote recomputes the 1-wei allocation to 0 and reverts at line 211. Attacker's original large vote weight remains unadjusted, inflating their share of bribes.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Replace `require(_poolWeight != 0, "ZV");` with `if (_poolWeight == 0) continue;` so dust allocations are silently skipped instead of reverting the whole operation.

ground_truth.description: Before describing the vulnerability, we should know that in ve3.3 systems, `poke` is important to make anyone reflect the decaying vote weight to prevent users from being inactive on votes to have their full weight votes on a pool. In `VoterV3` users choose what pools they want to vote for and the contract retrieves their `ve` weight upon doing so: uint256 _weight = IVotingEscrow(_ve).balanceOfNFT(_tokenId); And upon voting for a pool, that weight affects the claimable share distribution of that pool compared to other pools. Since now we know the importance of the voting weight, and since ve NFT weight decay with time, there is a poke function to update the voting weight made on a pool previously to the decayed weight of that NFT. The `poke()` function is guarded to be called by the owner or through the `ve` contract which can have anyone depositing for a user or increasing his locked value even by `1wei` to poke him to reflect his new decayed weight on the voted pools. An attacker can do the following: 1. vote his full weight - 1wei on a dedicated pool 2. vote 1 wei on another pool 3. time passes with inactivity from his side - his ve decay but is not reflected on voted pools 4. users try to poke() him through known functions of the ve contract 5. poke() function reverts here File: VoterV3.sol 208: uint256 _poolWeight = _weights[i] * _weight / _totalVoteWeight; 209:  210: require(votes[_tokenId][_pool] == 0, "ZV"); 211: require(_poolWeight != 0, "ZV"); Since the `1wei` vote multiplied by the decayed weight divided by totalVoteWeight rounds down to 0, hence this user becomes unpokable. Impact: The voted for pool will have inflated rewards distributed to him compared to other pools that have pokable users. Thinking of this attack at scale, the user will have advantage of having full voting weight if he votes immediately like having permanent lock weight without actually locking his balance permanently. Preventing anyone from preserving this invariant `A single veNFT’s total vote allocation ≤ its available voting power.` on his vote balance too.

ground_truth.attack_scenario: function test_dustVote_makesPokeDOS_dueToZeroPoolWeight() external { // Ensure BribeFactory is initialized so GaugeManager can create bribes during gauge creation BribeFactoryV3(address(bribeFactoryV3)).initialize( address(voter), address(gaugeManager), address(), address(tokenHandler) ); // Grant roles to allow token whitelisting and connector setup .setRoleFor(address(this), "GOVERNANCE"); .setRoleFor(address(this), "GENESIS_MANAGER"); // Whitelist tokens and set connector (HYBR as connector) address[] memory toks = new address[](3); toks[0] = address(hybr); toks[1] = address(gHybr); toks[2] = address(rewardHybr); tokenHandler.whitelistTokens(toks); tokenHandler.whitelistConnector(address(hybr)); // Create two pairs using HYBR as common connector token address pair0 = thenaFiFactory.createPair(address(hybr), address(gHybr), false); address pair1 = thenaFiFactory.createPair(address(hybr), address(rewardHybr), false); // Create gauges for both pairs so voter recognizes them as alive pools gaugeManager.createGauge(pair0, 0); gaugeManager.createGauge(pair1, 0); // Create a veNFT lock uint256 lockAmount = 1e18; hybr.approve(address(votingEscrow), lockAmount); uint tokenId = votingEscrow.create_lock(lockAmount, 2 weeks); // Vote with dust on one pool to set up zero rounding on subsequent poke address[] memory pools = new address[](2); pools[0] = pair0; pools[1] = pair1; uint256[] memory weights = new uint256[](2); weights[0] = 1e16 - 1; weights[1] = 1; // dust // Ensure we are past vote start window voter.vote(tokenId, pools, weights); // Advance time slightly so the NFT balance decays and dust path rounds to zero vm.warp(block.timestamp + 3); vm.expectRevert(bytes("ZV")); // _poolWeight != 0 reverts with "ZV" voter.poke(tokenId); }
ground_truth.fix_description: Change `require(_poolWeight != 0, "ZV")` to `if (_poolWeight == 0) continue;` to skip dust votes.

ground_truth.description: StakingBase._claim() and _withdraw() violate CEI by calling the virtual _transfer() function before updating persistent balance state. The virtual function can invoke token callbacks or receiver fallbacks, enabling reentrancy.
ground_truth.root_cause: StakingBase._claim() and _withdraw() violate CEI by calling the virtual _transfer() function before updating persistent balance state. The virtual function can invoke token callbacks or receiver fallbacks, enabling reentrancy.
ground_truth.attack_scenario: Attacker calls withdraw which triggers _transfer callback. During callback, attacker reenters to claim or withdraw again. State not yet updated from first call, so full balance is available for second extraction.
ground_truth.fix_description: Apply reentrancy guards to claim/withdraw/create. Reorder external interactions to follow CEI strictly.

ground_truth.description: The lock() function intends to lock the user's entire approved balance, but this will fail for the most common case: Most users give contracts they interact with an unlimited allowance by setting it to type(uint256).max. The _incomingTokenBalance() function at line 32 returns just 'erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this))' which would be type(uint256).max for unlimited approvals. The lock() function then attempts to transfer this impossible amount.

The _incomingTokenBalance() function at line 32 returns just 'erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this))' which would be type(uint256).max for unlimited approvals. The lock() function then attempts to transfer this impossible amount.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. User approves LockManager with unlimited allowance: approve(lockManager, type(uint256).max).
2. User calls lock() without specifying an amount.
3. _incomingTokenBalance() returns type(uint256).max.
4. _doLockTransfer attempts to transfer type(uint256).max tokens.
5. Transaction reverts because user doesn't have that many tokens.
6. User cannot use the standard lock() function.
ground_truth.fix_description: Have _incomingTokenBalance() return either the actual balance or the allowance depending on whichever is smallest: 'return (allowance >= balance) ? balance : allowance;'
